spans.text: Of the approximately 100,000 who emigrated, only about 7,300 (of whom 5,700 were black) actually went to the Bahamas, but this tripled the colony’s population, increased the proportion of blacks from one half to three quarters, and raised the number of permanently settled islands from three to a dozen (Craton & Saunders 1992: 179).

Nevertheless, the Bahamian economy was still far from being a typical plantation economy: Of a total of 988 persons living in the Bahamas in 1722, only 28% were listed as black, with percentages varying between 35% for New Providence and 4% for Harbour Island.
It was during the 1720s, after order had been restored, that the first substantial cargo of Africans (295 slaves from Guinea) was brought directly to the Bahamas (Craton & Saunders 1992: 119).
The country is heavily urbanized, with roughly two thirds of all Bahamians living in the capital, Nassau.

Historical and linguistic evidence (Hackert & Huber 2007; Hackert & Holm 2009) suggests that the Gullah-speaking areas, and South Carolina in particular, played a prominent role as a point of origin for both white and black loyalists, which makes it highly probable that what was taken to the Bahamas was an early form of Gullah rather than of African American Vernacular English, as had been assumed earlier (Holm 1983; Shilling 1984).

In any case, the Bahamian population grew; by 1671, when the first census was taken, it amounted to roughly a thousand (Craton 1968: 70).
